name: Arterial gas embolism
specialty: Diving and hyperbaric medicine / Emergency medicine

clinicalPearls: Gas bubbles entering the arterial circulation obstruct end-arteries, most dangerously in the brain and heart
In divers it classically follows pulmonary barotrauma during ascent, especially breath-holding on a rapid ascent
Symptoms are typically dramatic and immediate on or within minutes of surfacing, including loss of consciousness, seizures, focal deficits or cardiac arrest
It can also be iatrogenic, from vascular access, cardiac or pulmonary procedures and mechanical ventilation
High-flow oxygen and urgent recompression with hyperbaric oxygen are the definitive treatments
Any diver with neurological symptoms immediately after surfacing has gas embolism until proven otherwise
reference.pathophysiology: Arterial gas embolism occurs when gas enters the systemic arterial circulation and lodges in small arteries, causing mechanical obstruction, endothelial injury and secondary inflammation and thrombosis. In diving, alveolar rupture from lung overexpansion allows gas to enter the pulmonary veins and reach the systemic arteries, while iatrogenic cases arise from air introduced during procedures. Distribution of bubbles to the cerebral or coronary circulation produces the acute neurological and cardiac manifestations, and reduced perfusion beyond the obstruction drives ischaemic injury.
additionalInvestigations: Immediate clinical recognition based on timing after surfacing or a procedure
High-flow oxygen and preparation for recompression without delay
Assessment for pulmonary barotrauma including pneumothorax
Imaging as feasible, not allowing it to delay recompression
redFlags: Loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest on surfacing
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the bubble burden and speed of recompression; with prompt hyperbaric treatment many recover substantially, but delay or massive embolism can be fatal or leave permanent deficits.
pitfalls: Confusing it with decompression sickness and mismanaging the urgency
Missing a coexisting pneumothorax before recompression
Failing to give high-flow oxygen immediately
references: Diving and hyperbaric medicine references (standard reference)
management: Immediate administration of high-concentration oxygen to accelerate bubble resolution and treat ischaemia
Urgent hyperbaric oxygen recompression is the definitive treatment and should not be delayed
Supine positioning, airway protection and haemodynamic support, with advanced life support if cardiac arrest occurs
Intravenous fluids to maintain perfusion and counter endothelial injury
Identify and treat associated pulmonary barotrauma, including decompression of a pneumothorax
Arrange immediate transfer to a hyperbaric facility rather than allowing imaging to delay recompression
Continuous cardiac and neurological monitoring throughout treatment
Prevent recurrence through diving safety education and elimination of iatrogenic air sources during vascular access and procedures
